verdict.reasoning: Patient states, “I've really not been feeling so well at all recently. I've been struggling with fever for the past week… just generally not feeling good,” which supports fever and general malaise.

Patient reports “fever for the past week… it started about seven days ago,” plus “I'm really hot and sweaty all the time… aching all over… feeling quite nauseous… just generally quite tired and unwell,” matching a 7‑day history with hot sweats, muscle aches, nausea, and fatigue.

Patient describes “I'm sweating during the night. I'm quite cold” and confirms, “you're having periods of when you're feeling hot and also periods when you're feeling cold… Yes… it's quite interchangeable. Not really a pattern to it,” which matches sweating and chills without a specific pattern.

Patient says, “I've been trying to like take ibuprofen and paracetamol… but it's not really helping… Perhaps slightly, yes, but I'm still experiencing these symptoms, so it does take the edge off of it,” indicating slight relief.

Patient states, “I went to Vietnam. I came back four weeks ago now,” and describes trekking and cycling “through farmland… several different parts of the country in the countryside and some cities as well,” supporting recent return 4 weeks ago and rural activities.

Patient notes chronic back pain: “I've been struggling with back pain for quite a while,” is “under a physiotherapist at the moment,” and reports physio said it is “related to long periods of time sitting at a desk and just bad posture,” confirming posture-related chronic back pain with physiotherapy.
Medication list: “Are you on any medication at all? Patient: Just ceraset,” confirming current use of Ceraset.
Patient says, “I've been trying to like take ibuprofen… just from over the counter,” confirming OTC ibuprofen use.
Same sentence: “I've been trying to like take ibuprofen and paracetamol just from over the counter,” confirms OTC paracetamol use.

Allergy history: “Do you have any allergies…? Patient: No, I'm just really. Pollen allergy… Doctor: Okay, so hay fever? Patient: Yes. Yeah, just hay fever,” confirming pollen allergy with hay fever symptoms.
Family history: “The main one would be heart attack. My father passed away of that… Doctor: How old is he when that happens? Patient: 68, I think,” confirming father died of heart attack at 68.
Social history: “What do you work as? Patient: I work as a nurse,” confirming occupation.
Alcohol: “And do you drink much alcohol? Patient: Moderate alcohol intake,” matching moderate alcohol use.
Smoking: “Are you a smoker at all? Patient: No, I'm not,” confirming non‑smoker.
Exercise: “And how much kind of physical exercise do you do normally? Patient: I try and do some moderate physical exercise a few times a week,” confirming moderate exercise.
This was a teleconsult and no examination findings or vitals are mentioned anywhere in the transcript, so stating that no physical exam or vital signs are documented is consistent with the record.

Doctor notes need to “find a reason for why you've got this fever… Because there's no apparent reason from what you've told me,” which aligns with an assessment of fever without a clear source (fever of unknown origin at this stage).

Doctor states, “you've recently come from Vietnam… we need to think about things like malaria or other exotic infections as well,” directly considering possible tropical or other infections related to travel.

Doctor’s plan: “we need to think about things like malaria or other exotic infections as well… I'll be asking for something called thick and thin blood films to check for malaria and inflammatory markers and things like that,” indicating plan to rule out malaria and other exotic infections.
Doctor: “we're going to need to bring you into one of our clinics exam, and we're going to need to arrange some blood tests as well,” clearly arranging in‑clinic evaluation and blood tests.
Doctor: “I'll be asking for something called thick and thin blood films to check for malaria,” explicitly ordering malaria films.
Doctor adds, “and inflammatory markers and things like that,” which supports ordering inflammatory markers.

Doctor says, “I don't think you can go into work until we've sorted this out,” which is conditional on evaluation, not on symptom resolution. The fact claims advice “until symptoms resolve,” which changes the stated criterion.

Doctor: “You can come into one of our clinics in central London… What I'm going to do is I will send a message to one of our admin team members asking them to book you in,” which confirms coordinating an appointment in a central London clinic.
